The '''Women's Rugby World Cup''' is the [[women's rugby union]] [[world championship]] which is organised by [[World Rugby]]. The first Rugby World Cup for women was held in [[1991 Women's Rugby World Cup|1991]], but it was not until the [[1998 Women's Rugby World Cup|1998 tournament]] that the tournament received official backing from the International Rugby Board (IRB, now World Rugby); by 2009, the IRB had retroactively recognized the 1991 and 1994 tournaments and their champions.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.irb.com/newsmedia/mediazone/pressrelease/newsid=2033145.html|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131202230504/http://www.irb.com/newsmedia/mediazone/pressrelease/newsid%3D2033145.html|title=IRB press release|archivedate=2 December 2013}}</ref>

Normally, the tournament is held every four years; it was moved forward in 2017 so that the competition could be held in the year before the [[Commonwealth Games]]. The 2021 tournament was postponed to 2022 due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], but still marketed as the 2021 tournament.

Three countries have won the Women's Rugby World Cup since its establishment, with [[New Zealand women's national rugby union team|New Zealand]] having won the tournament a record six times followed by [[England women’s national rugby union team|England]] with three titles and the [[United States women's national rugby union team|United States]] with the single title in 1991.

==History==

===1990s===
Before the first Women's Rugby World Cup officially sanctioned by the International Rugby Board there had been three previous tournaments of a similar nature. The first of these was an event held in August 1990 in [[Rugby union in New Zealand|New Zealand]]. Though not considered a world cup, the tournament was referred to as the [[RugbyFest 1990|World Rugby Festival for Women]]. The competition included teams representing [[United States women's national rugby union team|the United States]], [[Netherlands women's national rugby union team|the Netherlands]], [[Russia women's national rugby union team|Russia]], and the hosts, [[New Zealand women's national rugby union team|New Zealand]] – who emerged as winners after defeating the United States in the final.

The first tournament referred to as the Women's Rugby World Cup was held in 1991 and hosted by [[Wales]]. Twelve countries were divided into four groups of three. The United States, against expectations, took the first championship with a 19–6 victory over [[England women's national rugby union team|England]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/rugby_union/international/1960497.stm|title=Women's Rugby World Cup – History|work=BBC Sport|pages=1|access-date=14 December 2008|date=13 May 2002|archive-date=26 February 2003|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030226084959/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/rugby_union/international/1960497.stm|url-status=live}}</ref> In the Plate competition [[Canada women's national rugby union team|Canada]] prevailed over [[Spain women's national rugby union team|Spain]] 18–4. Following the first tournament, it was decided to move the tournament schedule to the year prior to the next [[Rugby World Cup|men's world cup]], therefore reducing the quadrennial cycle to just three years.

The next event was originally scheduled to take place in [[Amsterdam]] but ended up being moved to [[Scotland women's national rugby union team|Scotland]]. Eleven countries competed in the tournament with the English meeting the United States in the final for the second time; however, in this instance England emerged as winners.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.uiweb.uidaho.edu/clubs/womens_rugby/RugbyRoot/rugby/games/Results/94WWC.html|title=1994 Women's Rugby World Cup – results|publisher=Uniweb|pages=1|access-date=14 December 2008}} {{Dead link|date=October 2010|bot=H3llBot}}</ref>

The 1998 tournament became the first women's world cup officially sanctioned by the [[World Rugby|International Rugby Board]]. [[Amsterdam]], who were originally scheduled to host the previous world cup, hosted the largest ever tournament with all matches played at the new National Rugby Centre in the city's west end.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://rugby.iespana.es/h3.htm|title=Rugby Femenino (Women's Rugby)|publisher=Iespena.es|pages=1|access-date=14 December 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091219110828/http://rugby.iespana.es/h3.htm|archive-date=19 December 2009}}</ref> The tournament also saw a record sixteen teams compete. New Zealand, who withdrew from the previous tournament, also competed. The final saw New Zealand defeat the United States and claim their first world cup title.

===2000–present===
The next event was taken to Spain in 2002. New Zealand won the title for the second time by defeating England 19–9 in the final.

The 2006 World Cup took place in [[Edmonton]], Canada, and was the first major international rugby union tournament and women's world cup held in North America. New Zealand defeated England in the final to win their third successive world cup title.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rwcwomens.com/EN/News/match_30.htm |title=New Zealand retain crown |publisher=International Rugby Board |pages=1 |access-date=14 December 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080723112527/http://www.rwcwomens.com/EN/News/match_30.htm |archive-date=23 July 2008 }}</ref>

[[File:Women's Rugby World Cup 2010, Wales v South Africa (5) - geograph.org.uk - 2030132.jpg|thumb|left|Wales v South Africa match in 2010]]
A record four countries expressed interest in hosting the 2010 World Cup. After considering bids from [[Rugby Football Union|England]], [[German Rugby Federation|Germany]], [[Kazakhstan Rugby Union|Kazakhstan]] and [[South African Rugby Union|South Africa]], the IRB announced that the 2010 event would take place in England.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/blog/2008/nov/12/rugbyunion1|title=Women's rugby looking to sidestep the doubters|work=The Guardian|pages=1|access-date=14 December 2008|location=London|first=Penny|last=Woods|date=12 November 2008|archive-date=12 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160812202212/https://www.theguardian.com/sport/blog/2008/nov/12/rugbyunion1|url-status=live}}</ref> The tournament was staged in London, with the final played at the [[Twickenham Stoop]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://users.ox.ac.uk/~ouwrugby/AhistoryoftheWomensRugbyWorldCup.shtml|title=History of the Women's Rugby World Cup|pages=1|access-date=14 December 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081212094016/http://users.ox.ac.uk/~ouwrugby/AhistoryoftheWomensRugbyWorldCup.shtml|archive-date=12 December 2008}}</ref>

[[File:Kendra Cocksedge and Stacey Waaka re-enacting celebrating the WRWC win.jpg|thumb|New Zealand celebrating their title in 2017]]
The [[2017 Women's Rugby World Cup|2017 World Cup]] was hosted by the [[Irish Rugby Football Union]], which governs the sport on an [[All-Ireland]] basis. Games were held in Dublin in the Republic of Ireland and in Belfast in Northern Ireland.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rte.ie/sport/rugby/2015/0513/700843-womens-rugby/ |title=Ireland to host 2017 Women's World Cup |publisher=[[RTÉ Sport]] |last=Ryan |first=Padraic |access-date=13 May 2015 |date=13 May 2015 |archive-date=8 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170808233532/https://www.rte.ie/sport/rugby/2015/0513/700843-womens-rugby/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://myguideireland.wordpress.com/2015/05/13/2017-womens-rugby-world-cup-to-be-held-in-ireland/|title=2017 Womens Rugby World Cup to be held in Ireland|date=13 May 2015|access-date=13 May 2015|archive-date=19 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150519002256/https://myguideireland.wordpress.com/2015/05/13/2017-womens-rugby-world-cup-to-be-held-in-ireland/|url-status=live}}</ref> The tournament was held one year earlier than usual in order to re-align the Women's Rugby World Cup's scheduling for greater synergy with the [[Summer Olympics]] (which added [[Rugby sevens at the Summer Olympics|rugby sevens]] in 2016) one year prior, and [[Rugby World Cup Sevens]] held the following year. The tournament was to return to a four-year cycle afterward,<ref>{{Cite news |date= 28 November 2014|title=Bidding process opened for 2017 Women's Rugby World Cup |url=https://www.insidethegames.biz/articles/1024073/bidding-process-opened-for-2017-women-s-rugby-world-cup |access-date=13 May 2022 |website=Inside the Games |archive-date=13 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220513031619/https://www.insidethegames.biz/articles/1024073/bidding-process-opened-for-2017-women-s-rugby-world-cup |url-status=live }}</ref> with the [[2021 Rugby World Cup]] awarded to New Zealand.<ref name="SportsPro-2019" />

[[File:RWC Women's logo.png|thumb|left|100px|Logo prior to 2021, when gender designation would be removed]]
In August 2019, World Rugby announced that in an effort to "elevate the profile of the women's game", the women's championship will be marketed under the "Rugby World Cup" branding, with no gender designation, beginning in 2021. World Rugby stated that the decision was intended to promote [[gender equality]] and "[eliminate] any inherent or perceived bias" towards men's events, with chairman [[Bill Beaumont]] explaining that it "demonstrates our ongoing and unwavering commitment to advancing women in rugby both on and off the field in line with our ambitious strategic plan." World Rugby became the first major sports federation to rebrand its events in such a way.<ref name="SportsPro-2019">{{Cite web |date=22 August 2019 |title=Top Story: World Rugby drops gender titles for World Cups |url=https://www.sportspromedia.com/news/world-rugby-drops-gender-titles-for-world-cups/ |access-date=13 May 2022 |website=SportsPro |language=en-GB |archive-date=19 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231019125059/https://www.sportspromedia.com/news/world-rugby-drops-gender-titles-for-world-cups/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The 2021 tournament in New Zealand was postponed by one year to 2022 due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]; it will still be branded as the 2021 Rugby World Cup.<ref>{{Cite news |title=2021 World Cup set to be postponed for year |language=en-GB |work=BBC Sport |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/56257270 |access-date=3 March 2021 |archive-date=13 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220513033619/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/56257270 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2025 the competition finals were expanded to 16 teams, from the 12 competing in 2021.<ref name="BBC Sport-2020">{{cite web |last1=Orchard |first1=Sara |title=Women's Rugby World Cup to expand to 16 teams from 2025 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/55129751 |work=BBC Sport |access-date=1 December 2020 |date=30 November 2020 |archive-date=30 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201130161221/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/55129751 |url-status=live }}</ref> On 12 May 2022, World Rugby announced that England, Australia and the United States would host the next three women's tournaments in [[2025 Women's Rugby World Cup|2025]], 2029, and 2033 respectively. As part of a new strategy, Australia and the United States were also awarded the preceding men's tournaments in 2027 and 2031 respectively—marking the first time that the men's and women's Rugby World Cup will be held successively in the same host nation.<ref>{{Cite web |date=12 May 2022 |title=U.S. to host 2031 and 2033 Rugby World Cups |url=https://www.espn.com/rugby/story/_/id/33896716/us-announced-hosts-2031-2033-rugby-world-cups |access-date=13 May 2022 |website=ESPN.com |language=en |archive-date=13 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220513031618/https://www.espn.com/rugby/story/_/id/33896716/us-announced-hosts-2031-2033-rugby-world-cups |url-status=live }}</ref>

In October 2023, as part of a new brand identity unveiled for the tournaments, World Rugby reversed its decision to drop the gender designation from the women's tournament, returning to the previous "Women's Rugby World Cup" title beginning 2025, but rebranding the Rugby World Cup as the "Men's Rugby World Cup" beginning 2027. World Rugby stated that the rebranding was meant to "promote unity across the tournament and provide clarity and consistency for fans".<ref>{{cite web |date=29 October 2023 |title=New visual identity revealed as Rugby World Cup embraces exciting future and rugby's unique energy |url=https://www.world.rugby/news/887975/new-visual-identity-revealed-as-rugby-world-cup-embraces-future-and-rugbys-unique-energy |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240925154023/https://www.world.rugby/news/887975/new-visual-identity-revealed-as-rugby-world-cup-embraces-future-and-rugbys-unique-energy |archive-date=25 September 2024 |access-date=25 September 2024 |website=www.world.rugby |publisher=World Rugby}}</ref>

==Results and records==
{{Main|
Records and statistics of the Women's Rugby World Cup}}

New Zealand have the most tournament wins, having won six times. England hold the record for most finals contested, having appeared in nine of the ten finals to date, and have been in the top three in every single tournament.

The record for most points overall is held by English player [[Emily Scarratt]], who has scored 175 during her World Cup career. She also holds the record for most points in one tournament, with 70 in [[2014 Women's Rugby World Cup|2014]].<ref name="Stats">{{Cite web|url=https://scrumhalfconnection.com/rugby-world-cup-womens-stats-archive/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20250619142825/https://scrumhalfconnection.com/rugby-world-cup-womens-stats-archive/|title=Rugby World Cup Women's Stats Archive|archivedate=19 June 2025|url-status=live}}</ref>

Canadian [[Magali Harvey]] holds the record for most points scored in a match by a single player, 41; she achieved this in the pool stage of the [[2017 Women's Rugby World Cup|2017 tournament]] against [[Hong Kong national rugby union team]]. Ireland's Realtine Shrieves holds the record for most penalty goals in a game, with five. New Zealand's [[Kendra Cocksedge]] holds the conversion record of 13 in a single fixture, in which her countrywoman [[Portia Woodman]] set the single-game try-scoring record of eight vs Hong Kong in 2017.<ref name="Stats"/>

Only five [[drop goal]]s have been scored in the history of the competition, one each by [[Elinor Snowsill]], [[Paula Chalmers]], [[Shelley Rae]], Amanda Bennett, and Carla Negri.<ref name="Stats"/>

New Zealand's [[Portia Woodman-Wickliffe]] holds the try record for both a single tournament (13 tries) and in a Rugby World Cup career (20 tries). Realtine Shrieves holds the single tournament penalty record with 11 successful kicks at goal in the 1998 edition. England's Emily Scarratt holds the penalty scoring record with 19 successful kicks across the 2014-2021 editions (she debuted in 2010 but did not take up goal-kicking duties until 2014).

Kendra Cocksedge holds the record for most conversions in a single tournament with 23 in the 2017 edition, while Emily Scarratt maintains the total record with 39 conversions.<ref name="Stats"/>

During the 2025 Women's Rugby World Cup, New Zealand's [[Braxton Sorensen-McGee]] and Canada's [[Julia Schell]] became the only female players to have scored two hat tricks in the tournament's history. Sorensen-McGee scored three tries in back to back matches against Japan and Ireland, and Schell produced a masterclass in scoring six tries (a double hat trick) in one match against Fiji. These are two of only three rugby players in history (men's and women's) to have achieved two hat tricks in one World Cup tournament, the other being former All Black winger Julian Savea in the men's 2015 World Cup.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-09-28|title= Braxton Sorensen-McGee: World Cup try leader, points leader, Breakthrough Player of the Year |website= [[Radio New Zealand]] |url= https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/574364/braxton-sorensen-mcgee-world-cup-try-leader-points-leader-breakthrough-player-of-the-year|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-08-24|title= Epic Double Hat Trick – Canada v Fiji – Rugby World Cup|website= [[YouTube]]|url=https://www.youtube.com/-kmQf_2to4k?si=2FxWZizIbQ-bhwwR}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-10-18|title= Records tumble in the All Blacks' Rugby World Cup quarterfinal win over France in Cardiff|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/sport/rugby/all-blacks/73123026/records-tumble-in-the-all-blacks-rugby-world-cup-quarterfinal-win-over-france-in-cardiff}}</ref>

The 1998 fixture between [[New Zealand women's national rugby union team|New Zealand]] and [[Germany women's national rugby union team|Germany]], with a final score of 134–6, set records for the highest combined points score (140), the most points scored by a single team (134), and the largest winning margin (128).<ref name="Stats"/>

==Format==
The format for the 2006 tournament split the 12 participating nations into four pools of three teams. Each nation played three games, after the completion of which a re-seeding process took place. Nations were moved into divisions dictated by their respective overall tournament ranking with the top teams proceeding to the knockout stages.

The 2010 event maintained the number of teams participating at twelve, with regional qualifying tournaments.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rugbyheaven.co.nz/4703895a22479.html|title=England to host Women's Rugby World Cup|publisher=rugbyheaven.co.nz|pages=1|access-date=15 December 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081017202240/http://www.rugbyheaven.co.nz/4703895a22479.html|archive-date=17 October 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref> The 2021 tournament retained the same format, but with the classification round replaced with quarter-finals, as with the men's Rugby World Cup.<ref>{{cite web |date=10 May 2018 |title=Women's Rugby World Cup: Format changes announced for 2021 tournament |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/44062807 |website=BBC Sport |access-date=22 August 2018 |archive-date=17 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180617091909/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/44062807 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Orchard |first=Sara |date=2018 |title=Women's Rugby World Cup: Format changes announced for 2021 tournament |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/44062807 |access-date=7 September 2018 |website=BBC |archive-date=7 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180907144714/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/44062807 |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2025, the tournament will expand to 16 teams.<ref name="BBC Sport-2020" />

== Trophy ==
The current trophy for the Winners of the Women's Rugby World Cup was made for the 2025 tournament in England. Designed and crafted by London silversmith's Thomas Lyte,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gabbitass |first=Anna-Rose |date=2025-06-23 |title=Thomas Lyte at the heart of the 2025 FEVO Sport Industry Awards |url=https://www.sportindustry.biz/news-categories/news/thomas-lyte-official-silverware-supplier-sport-industry-awards/ |access-date=2025-09-17 |website=Sport Industry Group |language=en-GB}}</ref> the trophy is made of sterling silver and plated with 24-carat gold. Made to stand at the same height as the Men's Rugby World Cup Trophy, the trophy is 38&nbsp;cm tall and weighs 4.5&nbsp;kg.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-08-22 |title=Women's Rugby World Cup: What does the new trophy look like? |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-union/articles/cvg30gj4dedo |access-date=2025-09-17 |website=BBC Sport |language=en-GB}}</ref> The design was selected by nine former world champions; [[Rachael Burford]], [[Gill Burns]], [[Monalisa Codling]], [[Katy Daley-McLean]], [[Fiao'o Fa'amausili]], [[Sarah Hunter]], [[Farah Palmer]], [[Anna Richards]] and [[Melodie Robinson]], and was selected to address criticism of the previous trophy being too small.<ref name="BBCNews2" />

There have been two previous trophies. The first was purchased for the [[1991 Women's Rugby World Cup]] by [[Sue Dorrington]] from JB Jewellery and Antiques in Hatton Garden for £1,007.50<ref name="WorldinTheirHands">{{cite book |last1=Thomas |first1=Martyn |title=World in Their Hands - The Story of the First Women's World Cup |date=2022 |publisher=Polaris Publishing Limited |location=Edinburgh}}</ref> and was one of the last items to be arranged for the World Cup. Dorrington was drawn to the intricate lace detail round the top of the trophy, but it later transpired this made it almost impossible to drink from. The trophy was awarded again at the [[1994 Women's Rugby World Cup]], but replaced for the [[1998 Women's Rugby World Cup|1998 edition]] when the IRB took over organisation of the competition.<ref name="RugbyPass1">{{cite web |last1=Heatly |first1=Gary |title=From Hatton Garden to parents' loft: Women's Rugby World Cup trophy history |url=https://www.rugbypass.com/news/from-hatton-garden-to-parents-loft-womens-rugby-world-cup-trophy-history/ |website=RugbyPass |access-date=30 September 2025 |date=14 May 2025}}</ref>

[[File:Black Ferns Ruahei Demant, Kennedy Simon, Georgia Ponsonby, Amy du Plessis standing with RWC trophy on parliament steps.jpg|thumb|Standing with [[2021 Rugby World Cup]] and medals on [[Parliament House, Wellington|parliament]] steps]]
The second trophy would be presented at the next seven tournaments up to and including the [[2021 Women's Rugby World Cup]]; won by [[New Zealand women's national rugby union team|New Zealand]]. This trophy was nicknamed 'Nancy' by the Black Ferns, who won it six times, in a reference to New Zealand World War II hero; [[Nancy Wake]].<ref name="BBCNews2">{{cite news |last1=Orchard |first1=Sara |title=New, bigger Women's Rugby World Cup trophy revealed |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/c62870j0wx6o |access-date=30 September 2025 |agency=BBC News |date=14 May 2025}}</ref>

After being replaced, the first trophy then went on tour, was displayed during road shows put on by the [[Rugby Football Union for Women]] and was also briefly on display at the [[World Rugby Museum]]. The trophy disappeared after going on tour in 2006 and it was assumed that it had been melted down.<ref name="RugbyPass1" /> Former Red Rose; [[Gill Burns]] had been searching for the trophy for several years until 2021 when it had been found in the loft of the parents of an England Rugby administrator; Helen Ames,<ref name="RugbyPass1" /> during a clear-out, it was then returned to the World Rugby Museum.<ref name="BBCNews1">{{cite news |title=Missing Women's Rugby World Cup trophy found in attic after 15 years |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/59011657 |access-date=30 September 2025 |agency=BBC News |date=22 October 2021}}</ref> It was later learnt through Phil McGowan at the [[World Rugby Museum]] that the trophy had been made in 1924.<ref name="RugbyPass1" />

The second trophy, after being retired, was also put on display at the World Rugby Museum.<ref name="RugbyPass1" />

==Media coverage==
The tournament has grown considerably in recent editions, with attendance more than tripling between [[2017 Women's Rugby World Cup|2017]] and [[2021 Rugby World Cup|2021]] editions, then again from 2021 to [[2025 Women's Rugby World Cup|2025]] which saw over four hundred thousand fans attend the tournament,<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.parallelparliament.co.uk/question/69613/rugby-world-cup | work=Parallel Parliament| title=Parliament Q: Rugby World Cup | date=21 July 2025 | access-date=10 March 2026 | archive-date=9 March 2026 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260309101439/https://www.parallelparliament.co.uk/question/69613/rugby-world-cup | url-status=live }}</ref> including record attendance for the competition at both the opening game,<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cn92pvd8ynvo | work=BBC | title=England open World Cup with 11-try win over USA | date=22 August 2025 | access-date=9 March 2026 | archive-date=5 March 2026 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260305034057/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cn92pvd8ynvo | url-status=live }}</ref> and the sold out final at [[Twickenham Stadium|Twickenham]].<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/czjvgj81y2mo | work=BBC | title=England overpower Canada to win Women's World Cup | date=27 September 2025 | access-date=9 March 2026 | archive-date=20 February 2026 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260220122739/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/czjvgj81y2mo | url-status=live }}</ref>

There has been commensurate growth with the television coverage, 1.3 million New Zealanders - over a quarter of the Kiwi population - watched the Black Ferns victory against the Red Roses during the 2021 edition.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/record-breaking-audience-for-black-ferns-rugby-world-cup-victory/EEWRSBBDGZBONFL5UYMUVCAIH4/ | work=NZ Herald| title=Record-breaking audience for Black Ferns Rugby World Cup victory
 | date=13 November 2025 | access-date=9 March 2026 | archive-date=6 April 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250406194257/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/record-breaking-audience-for-black-ferns-rugby-world-cup-victory/EEWRSBBDGZBONFL5UYMUVCAIH4/ | url-status=live }}</ref> During the 2025 edition TF1 saw 3.8 million viewers for France's semi-final clash with England,<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.sportcal.com/media/bbc-tf1-net-record-viewership-for-england-france-wrwc-semi/ | work=Sportcal| title=BBC, TF1 net record viewership for England-France WRWC semi
 | date=23 September 2025 | access-date=9 March 2026 | archive-date=18 November 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251118034601/https://www.sportcal.com/media/bbc-tf1-net-record-viewership-for-england-france-wrwc-semi/ | url-status=live }}</ref> and the BBC saw 5.8 million viewers for the final against Canada.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/mediacentre/2025/womens-rugby-world-cup-final-figures | work=BBC Media| title=Women's Rugby World Cup final smashes viewing records and becomes most-watched ever on UK television
 | date=28 September 2025 | access-date=9 March 2026 | archive-date=28 November 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251128180357/https://www.bbc.co.uk/mediacentre/2025/womens-rugby-world-cup-final-figures/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

In the United Kingdom, Sky Sports broadcast 13 live matches from the 2010 Women's Rugby World Cup, including the semi-finals, the third and fourth place play-off match and the final. The pool matches shown included all of England's matches, while each of the home nations' featured live too. There were also highlights shown from all other matches during the pool stages.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.skysports.com/story/0,19528,12328_6284813,00.html | work=Sky Sports | title=WRWC live on Sky! | date=20 August 2010 | access-date=29 July 2010 | archive-date=19 August 2010 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100819044317/http://www.skysports.com/story/0,19528,12328_6284813,00.html | url-status=live }}</ref> 
From 2017, the Women's Rugby World Cup was shown on free-to-air TV on ITV (2017–2021)<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.itv.com/rugby/articles/the-womens-rugby-world-cup-on-itv| work=ITV | title=https://www.itv.com/rugby/articles/the-womens-rugby-world-cup-on-itv
 | date=4 October 2022 | access-date=9 March 2026 | archive-date=20 April 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240420042749/https://www.itv.com/rugby/articles/the-womens-rugby-world-cup-on-itv | url-status=live }}</ref> and the BBC (2025—).<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.bbc.com/mediacentre/articles/2025/womens-rugby-world-cup-how-to-watch| work=BBC Media | title=Women’s Rugby World Cup 2025 Final Canada v England – Live on BBC One, iPlayer, Radio, BBC Sounds and BBC Sport Online
 | date=25 September 2025 | access-date=9 March 2026 | archive-date=23 August 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250823192111/https://www.bbc.com/mediacentre/articles/2025/womens-rugby-world-cup-how-to-watch | url-status=live }}</ref>

In Ireland the Women's Rugby World Cup was broadcast by [[TG4]] in 2014, the Irish language channel received praise for airing the tournament. TG4 provided coverage to all of the Irish matches as well as the final and semi-final.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.tg4.ie/en/corporate/news-releases/2014/170714.html |title=News Releases - 17.07 - Women's Rugby World Cup to be broadcast LIVE on TG4 - TG4 - Irish language television channel - Teilifis Gaeilge |access-date=19 February 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150510040058/http://www.tg4.ie/en/corporate/news-releases/2014/170714.html |archive-date=10 May 2015 }}</ref>
